rationale: B wins because it has tighter guardrails and better proof discipline, especially in "Whoop ships an FDA-cleared ECG and a blood-pressure feature that is deliberately not a medical device." A has the same basic shapes, but it dirties the file with "Whoop Finally Has FDA-Cleared ECG. Apple Watch Has Had It for Years." and then leans on competitor facts the update did not give it. B is not spotless — "a feature nobody has cleared" is an unsupported landmine — but it gives the founder cleaner strategic material.
gaps_in_A: "Whoop Finally Has FDA-Cleared ECG. Apple Watch Has Had It for Years." names Apple and asserts a timeline the supplied facts never gave. The update only says competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG.

"Apple Watch includes ECG with hardware, no subscription gate — confirm this" uses an unverified competitor-pricing claim as the spine of the access angle. If it needs confirmation, it is not ready to carry the story.
"The wearable industry has spent years positioning cuffless blood pressure monitoring as the next frontier" is a category thesis with no source in the update. Good instinct, unsupported execution.

"When a device can detect a condition linked to stroke and heart failure" adds medical context that may be true, but it is not in the update and needs sourcing before it goes near a health-equity pitch.
gaps_in_B: "blood pressure — a feature nobody has cleared" is too broad and unsupported. The update says Whoop's blood-pressure feature is not diagnostic; it does not say nobody has cleared one.
"at a company whose entire model is subscription rather than hardware margin" goes beyond the supplied facts. A premium-tier gate is supported; the full business-model claim is not.
"Health reporters are actively covering wearable-accuracy gaps" is a current media-landscape claim without evidence in the update. Useful as a research prompt, not as stated fact.

"the user who thinks they bought a blood-pressure monitor" overstates the consumer expectation unless Whoop's own marketing supports it. The safer story is the tension between the calibration requirement, wellness disclaimer, and buyer perception.
